📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Michigan's online casinos generated $305.3 million in adjusted gross receipts in October, up 16.7% from a year earlier. The double-digit gain comes as national iGaming growth cools, though Michigan's own pace has slowed from a year ago.

Michigan’s online casino market kept growing at a double-digit rate in October. Gross receipts came to $318.1 million, according to figures the Michigan Gaming Control Board released Nov. 18. It was the state’s second-best iGaming month of 2026. Only March, with a record $309.1 million in AGR, was higher. March also holds the monthly gross receipts record of $322.1 million, which topped the $315.8 million from December 2025.

The October result followed a soft patch. September AGR was $288.15 million, 0.9% lower than in August.

The year-over-year gain stands out against the national backdrop. Citizens JMP Securities estimated that US iGaming revenue grew 12% in the third quarter of 2026, the slowest pace it has recorded. Growth had been 19% in the first quarter and 16% in the second. The same data put Michigan’s third-quarter iGaming growth at 17%. Only Delaware, at 36%, and West Virginia, at 26%, grew faster.

Michigan’s own pace has still slowed sharply. In October 2025, online casino AGR grew 31.8% year over year, nearly double this October’s rate. That month produced $261.7 million in AGR and $278.5 million in gross receipts, a record at the time.

The Michigan figures also invite comparison with Pennsylvania. Its online casinos generated $278,845,570 in October revenue, a state record for Pennsylvania. That figure came in a release issued Nov. 17, a day before Michigan published its October numbers.

Sources indicate that the year-over-year numbers show where Michigan’s growth comes from. Online sports betting AGR fell 3.3% from October 2025. For all of 2025, sportsbooks produced $435.9 million in AGR, while iGaming generated $3.1 billion in gross receipts. Online casino play therefore accounts for most of the state’s online gambling revenue.

October sportsbook figures swung sharply from one month to the next. Sports betting AGR jumped 91.3% from September. Handle rose 11.1% to $605.4 million, and sportsbook gross receipts reached $70.7 million. Combined online casino and sports betting gross receipts totaled $388.8 million.

The broader online market had been growing faster earlier in the year. From January through July, combined online casino and sports betting AGR totaled $2.21 billion, up 20.9% from the same period in 2025. October’s casino growth is consistent with a market that is still expanding, but at a slower rate than a year ago.

Tribal online operators also made $8.9 million in payments to their governing bodies for October.

Google designed TPUs from the ground up to be exceptionally efficient for machine learning workloads, delivering top-tier performance per total cost of ownership (TCO). Because TPUs trade general-purpose hardware scheduling for wide systolic arrays, dedicated SparseCore engines, and custom interconnect fabrics, adhering to specific architectural best practices is essential to achieve maximum performance. To help developers get the most out of TPUs, we are launching the open-source AI-Hypercomputer/tpu-codesign guide. This post highlights its key principles—spanning shape alignment, architectural choices like LatentMoE, and parallelism strategies—to accelerate LLMs, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, and other hardware-intensive workloads on TPUs.

Performance tuning starts with model definition. Architectural choices made before the first training step set permanent ceilings on MFU (Model FLOP Utilization), cost, and serving latency. This guide gives concrete, hardware-grounded design rules for teams building or adapting models for TPUs, organized into three groups:.

In a recent development, how to use this guide. The shape rules apply to anyone designing a new model. If you are adapting an existing model rather than designing one, the Expressing Parallelism section applies without touching the checkpoint. The general rules hold for any large-matmul architecture (dense LLMs, multimodal, and world models), and the companion AI-Hypercomputer/tpu-codesign repository grows model- and workload-specific sections over time.

Eighth-generation TPUs. These principles carry forward to TPU 8t and TPU 8i and to the newly announced TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max. The reasoning stays the same and the thresholds move with the hardware. TPU 8t and TPU 8i both add native FP4. For training, TPU 8t also brings more balanced Vector Processing Unit (VPU) scaling. For serving, TPU 8i adds the Boardfly topology, a Collectives Acceleration Engine (CAE), and 3x more on-chip SRAM. We note the effects inline in Principles 5–8, and follow-up posts will cover eighth-generation designs in depth.

It has been revealed that measured evidence. Alongside the published sources, notes marked Measured carry results from our own Ironwood profiling program: open 20–30B MoEs (a Qwen3-30B-derived LatentMoE variant; GPT-OSS-20B) plus dense controls, single slice (except for the 512-chip TPU v7x and 1,024-chip TPU v4 ablations in Principle 4), BF16, training shapes up to 32K sequence, all against tuned-systems baselines. Treat the trends and rankings as transferable, the exact percentages as config-specific.

TPUs are purpose-built custom ML ASICs designed from the ground up to deliver state-of-the-art performance per total cost of ownership (TCO). While their architectural choices—such as wide 256×256 systolic arrays, software-managed VMEM, dedicated SparseCore engines, and direct multi-dimensional ICI fabrics—enable exceptional efficiency, they inherently create specific structural constraints and programming patterns that must be carefully followed to unlock maximal performance. Reaching peak efficiency requires aligning model shapes, routing, and parallelism directly with these underlying hardware characteristics:.

  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • It has been revealed that generating a single AI video clip is easy now.
  • It has been revealed that most guides stop at the clip.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that generating a single AI video clip is easy now. You send a prompt and get a few seconds of footage back. The trouble starts when the goal is three, five, or ten minutes of video where the same character looks the same in every scene, the style does not drift, and the captions line up with the picture.

It has been revealed that most guides stop at the clip. This one covers the part after it, treating a video as a small build pipeline: a storyboard that is data, prompts generated from that data, clips normalised and stitched with ffmpeg, and captions derived from the same source. If you want to wire a generation model into your own application first, SitePoint's guide to integrating generative video APIs into web applications covers the request and webhook side. If the finished video is headed to a YouTube channel, how to get a YouTube API key and use the Data API is a good starting point for the publishing side. Everything between those two is below.

Long-form AI video fails at the seams between clips, not inside them. Strategy for continuity before you generate anything.

A storyboard stored as JSON can be validated, versioned, diffed, and turned into prompts by code, which a pile of loose prompts cannot.

In a recent development, repeat the full character description in every prompt. Models do not remember the previous clip.

Clips from different generations rarely share resolution, frame rate, or codec settings. Normalise them before joining.

Captions are cheapest when generated from the script and measured clip durations, not transcribed afterwards.

Current video models generate short clips, commonly a handful of seconds each. A longer video is therefore many clips, and every clip is an independent generation. The model has no memory of what the character wore in the previous one.

Recent findings suggest that that produces three kinds of failure. The character drifts, so hair, clothing, or proportions change between scenes. The style drifts, so lighting and colour grade shift from cut to cut. And the technical specs drift, so one clip is 24 frames per second at one resolution and the next is something else. Each of these is fixable, but only if the project is organised so the fixes can be applied consistently.

Recent findings suggest that start with a structured storyboard instead of a document full of prompts. One file holds the style, a "character bible", and an ordered list of scenes.

"project": "rainy-day-lantern",.

"style": "soft watercolor picture book illustration, warm evening light, 16:9",.

"mira": "a nine year old girl with short curly black hair, a yellow raincoat and red rubber boots",.

"lantern": "a small round paper lantern with a gentle orange glow and a tiny smiling face".

"setting": "a narrow cobblestone street in light rain",.

"action": "walks slowly past closed shops, looking up at the sky",.

"camera": "slow push in from a medium shot",.

"narration": "It had rained all afternoon, and the street was quiet.".

"characters": ["mira", "lantern"],.

"setting": "under a bakery awning",.

"action": "finds the lantern glowing on a wooden crate and kneels beside it",.

"camera": "static medium close up",.

"narration": "Then she noticed something glowing under the awning.".

Because it is data, a script can check it before you spend any generation credits. Two checks pay for themselves quickly: every character named in a scene must exist in the bible, and no scene may be longer than the clip limit of the model you use.

const known = latest Set(Object.keys(board.characters));.

for (const scene of board.scenes) {.

for (const name of scene.characters) {.

errors.push${scene.id}: unknown character "${name}");.

if (scene.duration > MAX_CLIP_SECONDS) {.

${scene.id}: ${scene.duration}s is over the ${MAX_CLIP_SECONDS}s clip limit, split it into shots.

Recent findings suggest that treat MAX_CLIP_SECONDS as a setting. Limits differ between models and change over time, so check the one you are using rather than trusting the number in this example.

It has been revealed that never write the per-scene prompt by hand. Generate it, so the style line and the character descriptions are identical every time.

function buildPrompt(board, scene) {.

.map((name) => board.characters[name]).

It has been revealed that the character description appears word for word in every scene that includes that character. This is the single most effective consistency tactic that needs no special tooling. Changing a detail, say the colour of the boots, becomes one edit in the bible instead of a search through twenty prompts, and the diff shows exactly what changed between versions.

Put the style line first and keep it identical across all scenes.

Describe one action per clip. Two sequential actions in one prompt often produce a blend of both.

According to recent reports, keep camera directions simple. A single move per clip is more reliable than a combination.

Avoid naming real people, brands, or existing characters in prompts. Beyond the rights issue, it makes results harder to reproduce.

Clips from separate generations often disagree on resolution, frame rate, pixel format, or codec parameters. Joining them directly can produce stutters, green frames, or an outright error. Convert every clip to one agreed format first.

-vf "scale=1280:720:force_original_aspect_ratio=decrease,pad=1280:720:(ow-iw)/2:(oh-ih)/2,fps=24,format=yuv420p" \.

-an -c:v libx264 -crf 18 "norm/$(basename "$f")".

The filter scales each clip to fit a 1280 by 720 frame, adds padding if the aspect ratio differs, sets 24 frames per second, and forces a widely compatible pixel format. The -an flag drops any audio the model generated, since narration will be added as one track later. Name clips with zero padded numbers such as s01.mp4 and s02.mp4, so a shell glob sorts them in story order.

Once every file shares the same parameters, the concat demuxer can join them without re-encoding:.

for f in norm/*.mp4; do echo "file '$PWD/$f'"; done > list.txt.

ffmpeg -y -f concat -safe 0 -i list.txt -c copy stitched.mp4.

Recent findings suggest that hard cuts are the safe default. Crossfades are possible with ffmpeg's xfade filter, but they require careful offset arithmetic and a re-encode, so add them only when a cut genuinely looks wrong.

According to recent reports, captions are easiest when they come from the script, not from a speech recognition pass over the finished video. The storyboard already holds the narration text and each scene's length, so an SRT file is a few lines of code. Use measured durations rather than planned ones, because a generated clip is often a little shorter or longer than requested.

const out = execFileSync('ffprobe', [.

'-show_entries', 'format=duration',.

return Number(out.toString().trim());.

function toTimestamp(totalSeconds) {.

const ms = Math.round(totalSeconds * 1000);.

const h = String(Math.floor(ms / 3600000)).padStart(2, '0');.

const m = String(Math.floor((ms % 3600000) / 60000)).padStart(2, '0');.

const s = String(Math.floor((ms % 60000) / 1000)).padStart(2, '0');.

const rest = String(ms % 1000).padStart(3, '0');.

Recent findings suggest that update each scene's duration from measureSeconds on the normalised clip before calling buildSrt. If a narration line is long, split it across two caption blocks so it stays readable. Then combine picture, voiceover, and captions in one final step:.

ffmpeg -y -i stitched.mp4 -i narration.mp3 -i captions.srt \.

-c:v copy -c:a aac -c:s mov_text -shortest final.mp4.

Soft captions like these can be switched off by the viewer and read by assistive technology, which is better than burning text into the picture. Keep the .srt file as well, since most platforms accept it as a separate upload.

Recent findings suggest that everything above is a good fit when you need repeatability: many videos from templates, versioned storyboards, automated publishing, or tight control over the model. The price is that you own the glue code, the ffmpeg settings, and the failures.

For one off projects, or when the people making the video are not developers, a managed platform is often the more sensible choice. Tools such as magiclight.ai bundle story to video generation, character handling, voice, and an editor in one interface, and advertise videos of up to 50 minutes. Check the specifics yourself, because claims like that are marketing, and results depend on your content. One point matters for developers in particular: if you need to automate generation from your own code, confirm that the platform you pick offers an API or export route before you build a workflow around it. A tool with a good editor and no programmatic access suits a different job than the pipeline in this article.

Sources indicate that A short manual pass catches what automation does not. Watch the whole video once at normal speed, looking only at continuity. Read the captions against the audio. Check that no real person's likeness, brand mark, or protected character slipped into the footage. Finally, check the disclosure rules of the platform you publish on, since many now ask creators to label realistic synthetic media, and the rules change.

Industry observers note that the model is only one component of a long-form AI video. The reliability comes from the structure around it: a validated storyboard, prompts generated from it, clips forced into one format, and captions derived from measured data. Each of those is ordinary software engineering, and none of it depends on which generation model you choose, so the pipeline survives when the model changes.

According to recent reports, start with a two minute video and four or five scenes. Fix the seams there before scaling up, because every continuity problem you find at that size is one you will not have to hunt for in a ten minute project.

Utah sues Stake four days after the site added the state to its blocked list

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (538 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Readwrite

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Utah has sued the companies behind the Stake sweepstakes site, alleging it ran an illegal casino for Utahns since 2022.
  • It has been revealed that the timing of Utah’s suit against Stake stands out.
  • Sources indicate that utah Attorney General Derek Brown and the Utah Department of Commerce’s Division of Consumer Protection brought the case.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Utah has sued the companies behind the Stake sweepstakes site, alleging it ran an illegal casino for Utahns since 2022. The case follows Florida's own suit against Stake and adds to the legal pressure on the dual-currency sweepstakes model.

It has been revealed that the timing of Utah’s suit against Stake stands out. Stake added Utah to its list of restricted states on Nov. 13, four days before the suit was filed, yet state consumer protection investigators could still use the site as recently as Nov. 16, when a banner stated access would end on Dec. 7, the 43-page complaint indicates.

Sources indicate that utah Attorney General Derek Brown and the Utah Department of Commerce’s Division of Consumer Protection brought the case. It names two defendants: Sweepsteaks Limited, based in Cyprus, and its Australian parent, Easygo Group Holdings Pty Ltd. The state refers to them jointly as Stake.

The central allegation is that Stake has offered Utahns a round-the-clock casino since 2022. Utah has prohibited gambling since it became a state, and its Constitution bans gambling.

The complaint takes aim at how the site works. Players spend real money on two virtual currencies.

Recent findings suggest that utah wants the court to declare the site illegal gambling under state law. It also asks the court to bar Stake from offering its games in Utah and to order the company to return money taken from residents. The state is also seeking fines under the Utah Consumer Sales Practices Act and a remedy for harm to the public. The complaint adds claims for unjust enrichment, public nuisance and declaratory judgment.

A demand that players’ losses be repaid raises the stakes for the wider industry. Taken together, the relief Utah seeks increases the legal risk for sweepstakes operators, suppliers and affiliates nationwide.

Utah is not the only state to bring Stake itself into court. Florida’s suit is broader in scope. It names Sweepsteaks Ltd and Easygo alongside Medium Rare and Kick Streaming, NEXT.io reported. It also names co-founders Bijan Tehrani and Ed Craven, plus payment firms Praxis and Breeze Labs Payments. Utah’s complaint is limited to the two corporate defendants.

Other states have targeted the same business model through a different operator. Kentucky and Arkansas have both sued VGW, which runs its own dual-currency sweepstakes sites.

Sources indicate that the Stake case is separate from Utah’s clash with federal regulators over prediction markets. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has sued Utah to stop the state from using its own laws to shut down CFTC-registered contract markets. The Stake suit also came less than three weeks after Utah filed criminal charges against Kalshi’s founders. Those charges include felony counts of online gambling promotion.

Court records did not list a lawyer for either defendant, and the company did not answer a request for comment on the suit.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, connecticut's online casino revenue reached a upcoming high in October 2026, the first month taxed at a higher rate.
  • Connecticut’s two online casino operators, DraftKings and FanDuel, beat the previous record of $59.7 million, set in March, by about 10%.
  • Online casino handle topped $2 billion for the first time and was up 10% from October 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, connecticut's online casino revenue reached a upcoming high in October 2026, the first month taxed at a higher rate. Growth in the state sped up while the national market has been cooling.

Connecticut’s two online casino operators, DraftKings and FanDuel, beat the previous record of $59.7 million, set in March, by about 10%. October revenue was also nearly $10 million higher than September’s total.

Wagering grew as well. Online casino handle topped $2 billion for the first time and was up 10% from October 2025. Revenue grew faster than handle in the month. That is consistent with operators keeping a larger share of each dollar wagered.

It has been revealed that the October result runs against a cooling national picture. US iGaming revenue grew 12% year over year in Q3 2026, the slowest rate on record, SiGMA World reported. Connecticut grew at that same 12% pace in the quarter.

The American Gaming Association’s tracker reveals US iGaming revenue hit a record $3.05 billion in Q3 2026, up 13.5%. That was still the slowest quarterly growth since 2018. Connecticut had been part of the stronger phase. Its iGaming revenue reached $707.5 million in 2025, a 31.7% increase from 2024.

The jump from single-digit growth in September to a new high a month later stands out. It suggests the national slowdown is not uniform across states. One month, however, does not set a trend.

Operators paid the state 18% of online casino gross gaming revenue through September 2026. They owe 20% for every period after that, the Department of Consumer Protection’s dataset notes show. That lower rate covered the five years after online casino gaming began on October 12, 2021.

Recent findings suggest that the state’s take was already sizable before the increase. Online casino operators paid Connecticut $108,265,925 in 2025. Operators can still deduct some promotional credits before tax. That deduction has been capped at 15% of win since October 2023.

October’s figures show the higher rate did not coincide with any immediate drop in revenue. That matters for other states weighing online casino tax rates. It also matters for the two operators, which now share a larger tax bill in a market they split almost evenly.

Connecticut online casino wagers passed $2 billion in October, a record, in the first month taxed at 20% rather than 18%, according to state data. pic.twitter.com/FpO6DdEDUU.

— iGaming Times (@igaming_times) November 19, 2026.

According to recent reports, october was only the second month in the past 12 in which DraftKings, rather than FanDuel, took the larger share of Connecticut online casino revenue, according to Poker Industry PRO. FanDuel has led the state in most months over that period.

According to recent reports, operators must send each month’s online casino payment to the state by the 15th of the following month. The first payment at the 20% rate was due by November 15, 2026. Payments on November revenue fall due by the 15th of December.

Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Readwrite ↗ Open Full Page

Senate passes DEATH BETS Act to ban death and war prediction contracts in law

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (559 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Readwrite

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the US Senate has unanimously passed a bill that would ban death, war and terrorism contracts on CFTC-registered prediction-market exchanges.
  • Adam Schiff and John Curtis are the sponsors of the DEATH BETS Act.
  • Sources indicate that under the measure, any exchange registered with the CFTC would lose the ability to list or clear contracts on a person’s death, terrorism, assassination, war or US military operations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the US Senate has unanimously passed a bill that would ban death, war and terrorism contracts on CFTC-registered prediction-market exchanges. The vote would turn regulatory discretion into a statutory ban just as the CFTC proposes looser rules, and the House has only weeks to act.

It has been revealed that sens. Adam Schiff and John Curtis are the sponsors of the DEATH BETS Act. It is the first prediction-market bill the Senate has passed this Congress. The measure now heads to the House.

Sources indicate that under the measure, any exchange registered with the CFTC would lose the ability to list or clear contracts on a person’s death, terrorism, assassination, war or US military operations. Sports contracts are not covered.

Curtis made a moral case for the bill on the Senate floor. “There should be no financial incentive to profit from terrorism, war, or the death of another human being,” he mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that whether such contracts can trade currently rests on the CFTC’s discretion. The bill would replace that discretion with a prohibition written into statute.

The timing puts lawmakers and the regulator on different tracks. CFTC Chair Selig intends to rewrite the prediction-market rules. The agency’s proposed rule would amend Regulation 40.11 and add Appendix F to Part 40. The agency would use that framework to decide when a contract linked to war, terrorism, assassination, gaming or illegal conduct is against the public interest.

Recent findings suggest that that framework would give the agency more room, not less. The proposal would say only that the CFTC may find such contracts contrary to the public interest, dropping the categorical prohibitions in the current rule, according to the Congressional Research Service. The agency withdrew a stricter 2024 proposal in February 2026.

Industry observers note that for exchanges, the difference is significant. An agency can revise a rule through its own process. A ban in statute would keep those categories off the table regardless of how the CFTC’s rules change.

In a recent development, the DEATH BETS Act targets a specific set of contracts. Sports is a different matter for operators. Schiff and Curtis have also introduced the Prediction Markets Are Gambling Act. That bill would bar sports-betting and casino-style contracts on these exchanges.

A unanimous vote on death and war contracts does not prove the same support exists for a sports ban. It does show that senators are willing to legislate directly on what prediction markets can list, rather than leave the question to the CFTC.

That makes the vote an early sign of how much support Congress has for limiting these platforms. It comes while the exchanges are fighting state gambling regulators in court. Operators now face pressure from state regulators, the CFTC’s rulemaking and Congress at the same time.

The House now has a short window. So far, the chamber’s leadership has given no word on putting the bill to a floor vote, FinanceFeeds reported.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two federal judges have now declined to protect Kalshi from New York's state-court gambling enforcement.
  • District Judge Lorna Schofield denied the CFTC’s renewed emergency request on Friday, November 20, after a telephone hearing that began at 5 p.m.
  • Schofield found the CFTC was unlikely to show that the Commodity Exchange Act overrides state gambling laws.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two federal judges have now declined to protect Kalshi from New York's state-court gambling enforcement. The case moves to a state judge, and Kalshi disputes how far the proposed order would reach beyond New York.

Recent findings suggest that U.S. District Judge Lorna Schofield denied the CFTC’s renewed emergency request on Friday, November 20, after a telephone hearing that began at 5 p.m. ET, ruling from the bench in Manhattan.

Schofield found the CFTC was unlikely to show that the Commodity Exchange Act overrides state gambling laws. That includes licensing rules applied to prediction market operators. Her ruling came a day after Judge Vernon Broderick sent the case back to state court.

Recent findings suggest that the agency’s earlier bid had gone before U.S. District Judge Jed Rakoff.

With the federal route closed for now, the case sits with Justice Melissa Crane of Newly introduced York County Supreme Court.

Industry observers note that the proposed order would bar Kalshi from running an unlicensed gambling business within or from New York, or for people in the state. It covers sports, culture, election and other event contracts. It would also block users under 21 from trading.

The reach of that language is Kalshi’s central concern. In a Thursday-night letter to Crane, Kalshi’s Milbank lawyer Sean Murphy warned that the order would close the exchange to all customers everywhere, because the organization is based in New York. The letter also pointed to the likely forced liquidation of all open positions. James’s office has said that shutting Kalshi down nationwide is not what it is after.

Sources indicate that the CFTC has tried to place event contracts beyond state reach. On April 24, 2026, it sued New York in the Southern District of New York. It sought a declaration that it alone regulates event contracts. Similar suits had already targeted Arizona, Connecticut and Illinois.

On August 11, the agency issued an emergency order telling Kalshi to keep performing its functions as a designated contract market. Kalshi had warned the CFTC on August 1 that New York’s pending motion created a market emergency. The order was meant to reassure traders that one state cannot shut down a CFTC-registered exchange.

The financial exposure is large. New York seeks a permanent injunction and full restitution to people. It also wants a $100,000 penalty for each attempt to offer sports wagering, plus a further penalty of three times Kalshi’s gains.

Sources indicate that the case lands on top of a 3-1 run of federal appeals court rulings against Kalshi. That record raises the chance the Supreme Court takes up whether states can regulate prediction markets. Separately, the Second Circuit denied relief on November 3 in Kalshi’s own suit against New York regulators.

#184250. Tech Report: Your AI Pipeline Works. But Can You Trust It?

Tech Report: Your AI Pipeline Works. But Can You Trust It?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2947 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

AI is becoming a part of almost everything we do in technology today. Whether it's detecting fraudulent transactions, assessing credit risk, forecasting demand, or personalizing customer experiences, organizations are increasingly relying on AI to make faster and smarter decisions.

And naturally, when we talk about building AI systems, most of the conversation revolves around model accuracy, performance, and deployment. We spend considerable time making sure our models are trained well, our pipelines run efficiently, and our systems can handle production workloads.

But here's something we don't always pay enough attention to: Can we actually trust the data feeding these models?

According to recent reports, after all, even the most sophisticated AI model can produce misleading results if the underlying data is incomplete, inconsistent, or incorrectly interpreted. What's interesting is that these problems don't always show up as technical failures. Sometimes, everything appears to be working perfectly fine.

Imagine a financial institution that has recently deployed an AI-powered loan risk assessment system. The team has spent months preparing the data, training the model, testing its performance, and finally moving it into production.

The deployment goes smoothly. Data pipelines are running on schedule, predictions are being generated, and all the monitoring dashboards are green.

It has been revealed that A few weeks later, however, the business team notices something unusual. The model has started classifying more customers as high risk than expected.

The data science team checks the model configuration. Nothing has changed. The engineering team reviews the pipelines. All jobs have completed successfully. Even the infrastructure looks healthy.

It turns out that an upstream source system changed the definition of a customer income field from annual gross income to annual net income. The field name remained the same, the data type was still numeric, and none of the existing technical validations detected the change.

The pipeline continued running as expected, but the model was now receiving information with a different business meaning.

This brings us to an important point: Just because an AI pipeline runs successfully doesn't necessarily mean we can trust its output.

Building reliable AI systems requires us to look beyond the model itself. We need to understand where the data originates, how it changes as it moves through different systems, whether it meets quality expectations, and who is responsible when something goes wrong.

In this article, we'll explore three key elements of trustworthy AI pipelines (data quality, data lineage, and accountability) and look at how engineering teams can incorporate them into their existing workflows without making the process unnecessarily complicated.

Most modern data pipelines come with some form of operational monitoring. Engineering teams track job completion, execution time, system availability, and processing failures.

These metrics are vital because they help us understand whether our systems are functioning as expected.

Sources indicate that operational monitoring primarily tells us whether a pipeline executed successfully. It doesn't necessarily tell us whether the data being processed is accurate, consistent, or suitable for the model consuming it.

Suppose we're building a loan risk model that uses a customer's debt-to-income ratio as one of its input features.

The calculation is straightforward:.

Debt-to-income ratio = Monthly debt payments / Monthly income.

Now imagine that an upstream system starts supplying annual income instead of monthly income.

The calculation still executes successfully. The values are numeric, the transformation doesn't throw an error, and the model continues generating predictions.

However, the resulting debt-to-income ratio is incorrect because the numerator and denominator represent different time periods.

This is where traditional monitoring falls short.

To build trustworthy AI pipelines, we need to look at different dimensions of system health.

These approaches complement each other.

A pipeline can be operationally healthy while processing unreliable data. Similarly, a model can continue producing predictions even when the meaning of an vital input field has changed.

For engineering teams, the objective should be to identify these problems as early as possible, ideally before they reach downstream models.

We've all heard the phrase "garbage in, garbage out.".

And despite all the progress we've made in artificial intelligence, this principle hasn't changed.

AI models may be capable of processing enormous volumes of data and identifying complex patterns, but they cannot automatically guarantee that the information they're receiving is correct.

This is where data quality becomes crucial.

According to recent reports, data quality refers to how well information meets the requirements of its intended use. In AI pipelines, it helps us determine whether incoming data is sufficiently reliable for model training, evaluation, or inference.

Let's look at four dimensions that are particularly relevant.

Imagine we're developing a loan risk model that relies on customer income, outstanding debt, repayment history, and credit utilization.

What happens if 20% of the incoming records are missing income information?

Should we reject those records? Should we replace missing values using an approved statistical method? Or should we flag them for additional review?

There isn't one answer that works for every system.

The right approach depends on the model, the business requirements, and the potential consequences of the decision.

What matters is that missing information is handled deliberately.

For example, replacing missing income with zero may allow the pipeline to continue running, but it could significantly distort the model's predictions.

Validity checks whether values meet expected formats, ranges, and business rules.

Consider a customer record containing the following information:.

The credit utilization value immediately stands out.

Although credit utilization can exceed 100% in certain circumstances, a value of 450% may warrant investigation.

This highlights an important distinction: Not every unusual value is incorrect, and not every technically valid value is meaningful.

A database may accept any numeric value, but the business may need additional rules to determine whether that value is appropriate for the model.

Engineering teams should distinguish between invalid records, unexpected observations, and legitimate exceptions.

This is one of the most common challenges in enterprise data environments.

Imagine two systems providing customer income information.

System A reports annual gross income.

System B reports monthly net income.

Both datasets contain a column called income.

If we combine these datasets without understanding their definitions, we risk introducing inconsistencies into downstream calculations.

The data may look perfectly fine from a technical perspective. The problem is that the same field represents different business concepts.

This is why data definitions, units, and transformation rules are just as important as schema validation.

Suppose a model predicts a customer's current financial risk using income information that was last updated 18 months ago.

The data might be accurate, complete, and consistent.

But is it current enough to support the decision?

Different AI applications have different freshness requirements.

A real-time fraud detection model may require near-real-time transaction information, while a long-term forecasting model may work with less frequently updated datasets.

The important thing is to define these expectations based on how the data will be used.

The good news is that improving data quality doesn't always require sophisticated enterprise tools.

A practical starting point is to define validation rules for the most notable input fields.

For example, consider the following conceptual configuration:.

This is an illustrative data quality contract rather than executable configuration for a particular framework.

It defines basic expectations and specifies what should happen when the data fails validation.

Recent findings suggest that tools such as Great Expectations can help automate these checks. For smaller systems, custom SQL or Python validations may be sufficient.

However, technical validation alone isn't enough.

Remember our original example where the income field changed from gross to net income?

Both values could easily pass a rule requiring income to be greater than zero.

Detecting that kind of issue requires clear business definitions, communication with upstream systems, and appropriate change management.

In other words, data quality isn't just about checking values. It's also about understanding what those values represent.

Now let's assume our loan risk model generates an unexpectedly high risk score for a customer.

The model output is available, but we want to understand what contributed to the prediction.

We start investigating the input data.

The income information came from a customer application system. Outstanding debt came from another database. Both datasets went through several transformations before reaching the feature engineering pipeline.

The final features were then passed to the model.

At this point, a seemingly simple question becomes surprisingly difficult:.

Where exactly did the information used for this prediction come from?

This is where data lineage becomes valuable.

Data lineage describes how data originates, moves, and changes across different systems.

For AI pipelines, it helps us understand the journey from raw source data to the features used by a model.

A simplified flow might look like this:.

Source Systems → Data Transformation → Feature Engineering → Model Inference → Predictions.

Each stage introduces dependencies that can affect downstream results.

Data lineage can be captured at different levels of detail.

Dataset-level lineage shows relationships between datasets.

Loan Applications → Cleaned Applications → Model Features.

This helps us understand how datasets move through the overall architecture.

However, suppose the model's debt-to-income ratio suddenly changes.

Dataset-level lineage might tell us which datasets were involved, but it may not provide enough detail to identify the affected field.

That's where column-level lineage becomes useful.

debt_to_income_ratio = monthly_debt_payment / monthly_income.

Column-level lineage can show that the resulting feature depends on two upstream attributes.

If one of those attributes changes, engineers can trace the dependency and investigate the impact.

This is especially valuable in environments where multiple reports, applications, and AI models depend on shared data sources.

Large organizations may use dedicated metadata management and lineage platforms.

However, smaller teams can start by capturing essential metadata during pipeline execution.

OpenLineage provides an open standard for collecting and exchanging lineage metadata across supported systems.

For more detailed prediction-level investigations, teams may also need to retain feature snapshots or inference logs, subject to privacy and retention requirements.

It's key to understand that lineage doesn't automatically guarantee data accuracy.

A pipeline can be perfectly documented and still contain incorrect transformation logic.

But when something goes wrong, lineage gives engineering teams a clearer starting point for investigation.

Instead of searching across multiple systems and trying to reconstruct dependencies manually, they can identify where data originated and how it changed along the way.

Let's consider another situation.

An AI model starts producing unexpected results.

The data science team checks the model and finds no challenges.

The data engineering team confirms that the pipelines are running successfully.

The source-system team verifies that data was delivered according to its interface.

Yet the problem remains unresolved.

Everyone has completed their individual checks, but nobody has identified who should coordinate the investigation.

This is where accountability becomes important.

AI pipelines often involve multiple teams responsible for different stages of the data lifecycle. Without clearly defined ownership, even relatively simple complications can take longer to resolve.

A practical accountability framework should distinguish between three responsibilities.

Data owners are responsible for defining the business meaning and expected quality of critical information.

For example, someone needs to determine whether an income field represents gross income, net income, or another financial measure.

These definitions should be documented and communicated to downstream consumers.

Data engineering and platform teams typically manage data ingestion, transformations, validation mechanisms, and pipeline operations.

Their responsibilities may include implementing quality checks, monitoring failures, and assessing the technical impact of changes.

However, technical teams shouldn't be expected to make business-definition decisions without appropriate input.

Data science and ML engineering teams are responsible for evaluating model behavior, managing model versions, and assessing how changes in input data may affect predictions.

If a critical feature changes, the model team may need to determine whether additional testing, recalibration, or retraining is required.

Defining ownership is useful, but connecting it to an operational process is even more crucial.

Consider a critical data quality failure during feature generation.

A response process might look like this:.

The exact workflow will vary depending on the organization and the risk associated with the application.

The objective is to ensure that technical alerts lead to clear actions.

After all, an alert that nobody owns is just another notification waiting to be ignored.

So far, we've discussed why data quality, lineage, and accountability matter.

But how can we bring these concepts into everyday engineering practices?

Here are five controls that teams can introduce without redesigning their entire architecture.

Data contracts define expectations between data producers and consumers.

They can document schemas, field definitions, units, freshness requirements, and compatibility expectations.

For example, rather than specifying only that annual_income is numeric, a contract should clarify whether it represents gross or net income, the currency, and the applicable time period.

This reduces the risk of downstream systems misinterpreting technically valid information.

Quality gates validate critical data before it progresses through the pipeline.

These checks can be implemented during ingestion, transformation, feature generation, or inference.

For example, a feature engineering process calculating debt-to-income ratios should verify that debt and income values use compatible time periods.

Failure handling should reflect the severity of the concern. Some records may be quarantined, while more serious failures may require stopping the pipeline.

Pipeline execution should produce sufficient metadata to identify source datasets, transformations, and downstream outputs.

Where appropriate, teams should also capture model and feature versions associated with predictions.

This information supports impact analysis, debugging, and investigation when unexpected results occur.

AI systems evolve continuously.

Datasets change, transformation logic is updated, features are modified, and models are retrained.

Versioning helps engineering teams understand which components were active at a particular point in time.

Relevant evidence may include pipeline configurations, dataset snapshots, model versions, validation outcomes, and deployment records.

Retention should be designed around operational requirements, privacy considerations, and applicable policies rather than storing everything indefinitely.

Every critical data element or pipeline component should have an identified owner or responsible team.

More importantly, ownership should connect directly to incident management and change approval processes.

If a source definition changes, teams should know who evaluates the impact.

If a quality gate fails, the responsible team should receive the alert.

If model performance deteriorates, the investigation should have a clear escalation path.

These controls are most effective when they become part of normal development and deployment practices rather than separate administrative activities.

Implementing comprehensive governance across an entire data environment can be challenging, particularly for organizations with legacy systems and complex dependencies.

A more effective approach is to begin with one critical AI pipeline.

For example, a team operating a loan risk model could start by identifying the inputs that have the greatest influence on its predictions.

These might include income, outstanding debt, repayment history, and credit utilization.

For each critical input, the team can document five things:.

Once these foundations are established, the team can implement automated checks and gradually extend the approach to additional datasets.

This incremental strategy also makes it easier to demonstrate the value of governance controls.

For instance, teams can track how quickly data-related incidents are detected, how long investigations take, and whether recurring problems are reduced.

The goal isn't to introduce governance for its own sake.

It's to improve the reliability, maintainability, and transparency of the systems developers are responsible for operating.

Explainable AI has become an vital topic in machine learning.

Techniques such as feature importance analysis and SHAP can help teams understand which inputs influence model predictions.

However, explainability and data trustworthiness address different problems.

Suppose a model explanation identifies debt-to-income ratio as a major contributor to a customer's high-risk classification.

That explanation may accurately describe the model's behavior.

But if the debt-to-income ratio was calculated using an incorrectly defined income field, the explanation alone may not reveal the underlying data glitch.

This highlights the importance of evaluating AI systems across multiple dimensions.

Model explainability helps us understand how predictions are generated.

Data quality helps establish whether inputs satisfy defined expectations.

Data lineage provides visibility into where information originated and how it was transformed.

Accountability ensures that identified problems can be investigated and addressed.

These capabilities are complementary rather than interchangeable.

Sources indicate that none independently guarantees that an AI system is accurate, fair, secure, or compliant. Together, however, they provide a stronger foundation for evaluating and improving system reliability.

As AI systems become more integrated into business processes, engineering teams face increasing expectations around reliability, transparency, and accountability.

Model accuracy and operational performance remain essential, but they represent only part of the overall picture.

A pipeline can execute successfully while processing inconsistent information. A model can generate predictions using features whose definitions have changed. And an explanation can describe a model's behavior without identifying problems in the underlying data.

Building trustworthy AI therefore requires attention to the entire data lifecycle.

Data quality controls help detect unreliable inputs. Lineage provides visibility into how information moves through systems. Clear ownership ensures that complications can be investigated and resolved.

Importantly, these practices don't need to begin with large-scale governance programs or expensive technology investments.

Engineering teams can start with a single critical pipeline, identify its most notable data elements, establish quality expectations, and introduce basic traceability and accountability mechanisms.

Over time, these practices can become part of standard development and deployment workflows.

According to recent reports, the real measure of a trustworthy AI pipeline isn't simply whether it produces a prediction. It's whether the organization can understand, validate, and take responsibility for the information behind that prediction.

After all, a green dashboard is reassuring. But it shouldn't be the only evidence that an AI system is working as intended.

The newsletter officially kicks off on November 10th. That’s after a way-too-long four-year hiatus. What the heck, right? It’s not only high time for it to come back, but for you to get on the list. You’ll get hand-written and hand-curated news, links, and editorials that you can only find there. Join the party with me!

So, let’s go out with a big bang for our “final” concern. It’s packed with some stuff that I’ve been holding onto since before the site came back to life earlier this week, but also some upcoming stuff, and I can’t wait to finally get it out to you.

Industry observers note that scooch over Apple, Rockstar has something they’d like to say about fancy scrolling effects (to be fair, they’ve had 13 years to create them). First, check out the GTA 6 website (which oddly doesn’t work in Firefox), then watch Kevin Powell’s GTA 6 scroll effects walkthrough, which is frankly the most fun that you can have while waiting (and waiting) for GTA 6.

According to recent reports, mojtaba Seyedi demonstrated how to build a scrollspy with modern CSS. What’s a scrollspy, you ask? Well, if you have a navigation that links to different sections of the page, a scrollspy highlights the section that you’re right now on in the navigation.

Brecht De Ruyte showcased and explained some absolutely stunning random() demos.

Okay, that was more than a few….

Lea Verou explained, in detail, the different ways of implementing icons on the web. Many exciting CSS features of the future are mentioned, including Linked Parameters, ident(), @mixin and @apply, the @property shorthand, and more, so it’s a really deep dive with a lot of intrigue.

In a recent development, kilian Valkhof suggested a universal pseudo-selector. I mean, the universal selector (*) doesn’t select pseudo-elements, which is why almost every website uses the following CSS snippet, right?

But there are way more of them now (e.g., ::backdrop and ::details-content, to name just a couple of common ones in the context of box-sizing: border-box), so Kilian suggests ::*.

According to recent reports, declan Chidlow told us which latest HTML and CSS features are useful for design systems. My favorites are text-box, sibling-index(), sibling-count(), @scope, and @custom-media, which are very handy even outside of design systems.

#184242. Industry News: What to Check Before Adding a Tripo Model to a Website

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1473 w)

Industry News: What to Check Before Adding a Tripo Model to a Website

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1473 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • A 3D model can look convincing in a still image and still be awkward on a website.
  • Sources indicate that this article walks through a web-readiness review for an AI-generated model, using an openwork ceramic vessel generated from a single reference image with Tripo as the worked example.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

A 3D model can look convincing in a still image and still be awkward on a website. The real questions appear when someone rotates it, loads it on a typical connection, or views it on a narrow phone screen. AI generators have made the first draft of a model cheap, which shifts the work toward the part developers and designers already know: budgets, testing and fallbacks.

Sources indicate that this article walks through a web-readiness review for an AI-generated model, using an openwork ceramic vessel generated from a single reference image with Tripo as the worked example. The checks apply equally to output from other generators. It includes a small Node.js script that audits a GLB file against a size budget, and the markup for a lightweight viewer with a static fallback. The model shown is one candidate, so it cannot prove browser speed, mobile behavior, hidden geometry or export compatibility. Those are checks to run on your own asset.

Industry observers note that traditional 3D work involves modeling, polygon layout, materials, scale and export. AI generation can shorten the blank-workspace stage. A beginner may discover the category through a search such as AI 3D model generator free, but an initial candidate is useful only if it survives review.

Sources indicate that for this vessel, start with the negative space, meaning the openings between the ribs. A flattering front view can hide a blocked cavity, a thin wall, or two surfaces passing through each other. Generation moves the bottleneck from making a first shape to deciding whether that shape is usable.

Image-to-3D tools use a visual reference to create a model candidate, while text-to-3D routes start from a written prompt. Tripo offers both, and other hosted options include Meshy, Rodin by Hyper3D and 3D AI Studio, all of which list GLB among their export formats, while open-source models such as TripoSR and Stable Fast 3D let you run generation yourself. Features, pricing, licensing and output quality differ and change often, so check each vendor’s current documentation. The image route suits this example because the folds, uneven rim and openings already exist in the source.

Whichever tool you use, it can provide a candidate for inspection. It cannot decide whether the source is licensed, whether the unseen rear structure is believable, or whether the exported asset suits a particular viewer. Those judgments belong to the person publishing the page.

According to recent reports, give the object one job. In a portfolio, this vessel might show how its shell and openings relate. That is narrower than calling it printable, manufacturable or dimensionally accurate. Note what must remain recognizable, and provide a still image if the interactive view fails.

Use an image you own or have permission to reuse. Busy backgrounds can distract an image-based workflow, so isolate the object when possible. One photograph also leaves the back and underside unknown. Treat those areas as review risks, not as details confirmed by the source.

In a recent development, after generation, rotate beyond the familiar front. Check the rear, top, underside and sides. Trace each large opening. Look for merged ribs, intersecting surfaces or an unstable base. A wireframe view, when available, can expose crowded geometry. A single front-facing candidate cannot answer these hidden-angle questions, so check them on your own model.

Record the download size, polygon count and texture dimensions. Polygons are the small flat faces that form the shape, and web viewers draw them as triangles. This matters because generator defaults are often tuned for quality, not for the web. In the generation screenshot for this vessel, the viewer reports roughly 1.95 million faces and the settings show 4K texture quality. That is a fine starting point for inspection but a heavy asset for a phone on a mobile connection. Curved ribs may need many triangles, but the count should still fit your page budget.

glTF is the open format most web viewers expect, and GLB is its single-file form that can bundle geometry, textures and materials. The format does not guarantee good performance, so measure the package. The script below reads a GLB with the open-source glTF Transform library, counts triangles, lists texture sizes, and compares them with a budget. The budget values are placeholders; set your own from your target devices.

Run it with node audit.mjs model.glb after installing @gltf-transform/core. It exits with a non-zero status when the asset is over budget, so you can run it in CI. A short test builds two GLBs with known triangle counts, one small and one with 200,000 triangles, and checks that the first passes and the second fails with the right message:.

It has been revealed that when an asset fails, glTF Transform also has a command line. gltf-transform inspect model.glb reports what is inside a file, and gltf-transform optimize input.glb output.glb --compress draco --texture-compress webp applies geometry and texture compression. Compression and mesh simplification can introduce artifacts, especially around thin ribs and openings, so reopen the result and re-check the angles from Gate 3 instead of accepting a smaller file blindly. Also check that your viewer supports the compression you choose.

Load the asset in the intended viewer at desktop and phone widths. Check framing, touch rotation, keyboard access, scrolling and a slower connection. The Google-backed model-viewer web component is one low-code option, and libraries such as three.js give you more control at the cost of more code. The markup below demonstrates the pieces that matter for a first release: a poster image that loads first, lazy loading so the heavy file waits until needed, a text alternative, and visible controls.

The alt text, a poster and touch-action="pan-y" (so a vertical swipe still scrolls the page on a phone) address the common failures. Check the current model-viewer documentation for attribute names and the recommended script include, since they can change between versions. Also consider the WCAG guidance on non-text content: provide a useful description, and offer instructions plus a static image for people who cannot operate the viewer.

A single front-facing candidate is enough to discuss the method, not to certify a finished web asset. Call it a prototype until the exported file passes the checks required by its actual destination.

The same review pattern can be adapted to an architectural ornament, exhibition object, packaging concept or game prop, but each destination adds its own geometry, scale and delivery requirements. A portfolio may accept an inferred rear surface if that limitation is clear. A sales page, printable file or measured product needs stronger references and technical validation.

Sources indicate that the audit script counts triangles, texture sizes and file size only. It does not detect self-intersections, thin walls, flipped normals or licensing problems, and passing it does not make an asset good. The budget numbers are illustrative, and real limits depend on your audience’s devices and connections. Tool features and terms change, so verify them with the vendor before you rely on them, and treat any speed or quality claims on vendor pages as the vendor’s own.

Inspect the angle you would normally crop out. Confirm input rights, measure the download, and test touch, keyboard and a slow connection. Reread the surrounding copy, because claims of fabrication accuracy or production readiness need supporting evidence. For this vessel, “exploratory web model” is an honest label, and more demanding claims require better references and a specialist review.

Decide what visitors should learn or do before adding a 3D viewer. A modest prototype with a useful fallback can beat a dramatic asset that loads slowly or hides limitations.

Industry observers note that do I need to code to create a model with an AI generator? No code is required to generate an initial model candidate in Tripo or similar tools. Publishing it interactively is separate work and usually involves a viewer, hosting, responsive testing and enough HTML or JavaScript knowledge to diagnose problems.

When should I use image-to-3D instead of text-to-3D? Use image-to-3D when a rights-cleared visual should guide the form, and text-to-3D when the idea begins as words. Do not treat the two routes as interchangeable evidence.

Is a generated model ready to publish as soon as it exports? No. Inspect the shape from several angles, measure the delivery package, test the intended viewer and prepare a fallback. Higher-stakes uses may also need specialist geometry, scale, material and rights review.

It has been revealed that how can a beginner keep web 3D manageable? Give one object one clear job. Set a file-size target, test desktop and phone widths, keep interaction simple, and retain a still image for readers who cannot load or operate the viewer.

According to recent reports, the title sounds a bit strange, right? Why re-implement an existing feature, that’s completely useless! I have two reasons for that. The first reason is to be able to adjust the :nth-child() arguments on the fly.

Let’s suppose you have the following:.

And you decide to upgrade the 5 or the 8. The only way is to manually rewrite the selector, which isn’t ideal. We cannot have something like the below where you can change the variables as you want:.

The second reason is to have fun and play with some new features. You will probably never need to rely on a dynamic :nth-child() selector, but I am sure you will learn one or two useful tricks along the way.

We will rely on the same code structure in all the examples: a container with a bunch of elements inside it.

And the container controls the variables of :nth-child():.

In a recent development, I am not saying that this structure is mandatory for the implementation. I just considered a simple one to keep things easy to follow.

Let’s start with the simplest case, a selector that selects only one element:.

According to recent reports, I don’t think I need to explain what this selector does. The 5 is nothing but the index of the selected element. So, if B is equal to the index of the element, that element is selected.

We can translate this into the following CSS code:.

I am using the newly introduced if() syntax that allows me to define a condition within style(). If that condition is true, the background color is set to red. Otherwise, nothing happens.

The if() syntax is not that complex. In our case, we only have one condition, so you can see it as follows:.

The tricky part is how to define the condition within style(). I wrote a small post explaining this part, so do yourself a favor and go read it before we continue: “The Hidden Trick of Style Queries and if().” It’s a quick reading with crucial details that helps you better understand how if() works. From there, you will notice that our condition can be written several ways that are all valid:.

In a recent development, we have our first implementation! You can easily apply it to any property as well:.

In a recent development, the code looks a bit redundant, which is probably one of the drawbacks of this method, but it’s still cool to implement the selector and be able to adjust the value of --B on the fly. Don’t forget that our goal is to learn fresh tricks, and you already have two of them in your pocket (sibling-index() and if()).

Here is an interactive demo where you can adjust the value of --B and see the changes:.

Let’s move to our next selector. It selects more than one element.

Industry observers note that think for a moment about how to implement such a selector. It’s almost the same as the previous one.

If the index of the element is greater than or equal to the value of --B, the element is selected. As simple as that!

What about this one? Easy, right? We simply use <= instead of >=!

We can also easily implement a range selection, which is the combination of both selectors:.

The code should be self-explanatory. It’s even more intuitive than the :nth-child() notation, which requires a few minutes of deciphering if you are not used to it.

Sources indicate that now let’s deal with the A argument. For example, the following selector:.

Recent findings suggest that …selects the 3rd, 6th, 9th, etc. elements. Seen differently, the index of the element needs to be a multiple of 3. To do such testing, we can use the mod() function. If mod(index, 3) returns 0, it means the remainder of the division of index by 3 is equal to 0, hence, it’s a multiple of 3.

It works! Another selector with a simple implementation.

We can identify two special cases. When --A is equal to 1, we have :nth-child(n), which selects all the elements and when it’s equal to 2, we have :nth-child(2n) which is also :nth-child(even).

According to recent reports, while this works fine, there is a small gotcha. When A is a negative value, the selector should select nothing which is logical as all the indexes are positive, but if you try using negative values with my implementation, some elements still get selected which is wrong.

The mod() function works with negative numbers and can still return 0 in such cases, so to be more accurate, we should test the sign of A.

See that? I simply added another condition inside style() using the and keyword. The syntax of if() may sound confusing at first glance, but at the end it’s the same as any other language: a bunch of conditions defined inside style(). You can have as many as you want combined with and and or.

Now, our selection is more precise.

Recent findings suggest that now let’s combine all the tricks we learned so far to implement the generic form of :nth-child(). In this case, the index is equal to An + B, and we can express n like this:.

According to recent reports, n should be a positive integer (zero included). For the positive part, we can use:.

For the integer part, we need to make sure index - B is a multiple of A, and for this, we use mod():.

We translate this into CSS to get the following:.

Sources indicate that we are almost good except for the case when --A is equal to 0. In that case, the selection is simply wrong. The mod() results in NaN since its second argument is equal to 0, and this will mess with the condition. Actually, that condition is not meant to work with --A equal to 0.

We either consider that this implementation is only valid for a value of --A different from 0 (which is probably what we want) or we try to find a solution to include that case.

In a recent development, we are here to learn and discover new stuff, so let’s try something else. There are probably a lot of ways to fix the case of 0, but here is my idea:.

How does it work? Well, this will be your homework!

Recent findings suggest that as you can see, I have introduced a new variable that should be equal to 1 if the element is selected by :nth-child(An + B). Try to dissect the code to understand how it works. If you still struggle, check the following post: “Dynamic nth-child() using sibling-index() andif().”.

And here is the final interactive with the complete implementation of :nth-child(An + B):.

We can easily get all the previous selectors by simply adjusting the variables:.

Recent findings suggest that I hope you enjoyed this small exercise. It was a good opportunity to explore the new if() feature, and the :nth-child() selector was the perfect candidate for this. After all, selectors are nothing but a set of conditions to filter elements and select the needed ones.

What about :nth-last-child()? If you are up for another challenge, try to see how you can enhancement the previous implementation to make it work with :nth-last-child(). (Hint: you may need to rely on sibling-count().).

Industry News: What Is BIO Tagging and How to Use It for Document AI Training Data
